issues.title: Vice-Chair from IESG members
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
Suggestion received in email.

> appoint another AD at their discretion as Vice-Chair at the time the IETF Chair is appointed, so it's done in advance. Three steps:
>
>The IETF Chair is appointed.
>The IETF Chair chooses a Vice-Chair from IESG members.
>The IAB Chair steps in if both of these steps fail.

comments.author: becarpenter
comments.body: Good idea. It would avoid any delay in ongoing operations.

issues.title: Replace "Proposed"
issues.author: becarpenter
issues.body: Most of the uses of "propos*" and  "suggest*" should be replaced by a positive or normative word.

issues.title: I think you want the term "vice chair"
issues.author: sayrer
issues.body: The important part of this term is that they are designated in advance. It doesn't have to be anything dramatic to cause this process to kick in. It can just be a missed flight or a child's graduation, causing a scheduling conflict. That way, business can carry on. Most of it is uncontroversial. If there were something really serious, it would take a long time anyway, but all of the other regular business can get done.

comments.author: becarpenter
comments.body: Yes. It seems to me that it is standard practice throughout the real world to designate an alternate to take over when the principal is unavailable. There's nothing magical about the IETF Chair role in ths respect. The oddity is that we _don't_ identify a Vice-Chair.

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body: Yep, and "unavailable" is better than "incapacitated", which is way too loaded. I just got to Mirja's and Ekr's comments, which say the same thing. I think part of being the IETF Chair is to pick a good vice chair, which avoids Ekr's concern about an unappointed executive (not unappointed exactly, they are already an AD).

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body:
Maybe the thing to think about is whether we're just trying to look after everyday business or handle really exceptional cases. I think we should not aim for the latter, as there will probably be more than we can write if that happens.

There is a comparable historical case: many people think Gerald Ford was the Speaker of the House. No. Nixon's Vice-President resigned, the Congress confirmed the House Minority leader as VP, and then Nixon resigned.

That kind of thing can't be covered in a BCP, but we can do normal business if someone is unavailable without conducting an election. (see 12th amendment, a less known one)

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: I decided against "vice chair" on purpose, because I think it carries too much baggage (= implies there is more to this than we define here). "Vice chair" to me sounds like the role has ongoing duties, which it doesn't.

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body: Oh, but that's why it exists. If the chair is unavailable, they cannot delegate anything (Mirja's point on the mic). The idea is to let the boring stuff proceed if the chair is indisposed (maybe an even better word?). A wise Vice Chair would delay anything serious.

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body:
This is weird English, so just so it's super clear:

": slightly ill —often used to politely excuse someone's absence without giving a specific reason"

https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/indisposed

There's more to it, though. It can mean something like "someone rang the doorbell while you were in the shower". That's what we're after here. (the person is not incapacitated, it's just unreasonable to answer the door, even though they could)

comments.author: becarpenter
comments.body:
It seems to me that either "vice" or "deputy" would work, as long as it's defined in the text. That's the only way to avoid misinterpretation. Since we're all geeks here, we could even call them the "Backup Chair". In sports, they'd be the "Reserve Chair."

(Fred Baker would have been a great asset to this conversation, and I can almost hear him wryly observing that "Vice Chair" could be misunderstood as "Chair of Vice" - the word's double meaning might be confusing for some non-native speakers of English. So maybe "Deputy" is actually better.)

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body:
> It seems to me that either "vice" or "deputy" would work, as long as it's defined in the text. That's the only way to avoid misinterpretation. Since we're all geeks here, we could even call them the "Backup Chair". In sports, they'd be the "Reserve Chair."

To keep it light-hearted: although I think this issue is a serious point, it would be "backup" in American English sports. So, if you're watching Premier League football, you say "reserve striker", but you say "backup point guard" if you're watching the NBA.

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body: Both are wrong too, for this situation. Here, we want someone with the cool to say "oh, they're not here, let's do the boring stuff". There's no coach that decides to put them in. There's no Pep Guardiola.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Now that the drafts are split, it might make sense to see if the "vice chair" rename makes sense in the context of the "standin" draft.

comments.author: sayrer
comments.body:
It's here now:

https://github.com/ietf-wg-procon/ietf-chair-may-delegate/pull/31

If you use the term "vice-chair", it cleans up further. But there are two separate points.

issues.title: IAB Membership of the IETF Chair can not be delegated
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body: In the IAB charter RFC2850, the IETF Chair is called out as a member of the IAB and this is not just a role or responsibility that can be delegated. Similar as any IAB member cannot delegate its membership to someone else; especially any voting rights cannot be delegated. However, I also don’t think there is a need for delegation here. There is also the liaison from the IESG to the IAB; so there is also a second link between the groups. And similar as IAB members are potentially less active for some periods of time, it is also not a real problem if the IETF Chair would not be able to actively participate in IAB activities for a while; again the membership, however, remains, no matter if someone is actively contributing or not.

comments.author: jariarkko
comments.body: Agree

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: I agree that the IAB membership cannot _currently_ be delegated. I think you mean that this document (as an IETF-stream document) cannot change 2850 and that the IAB would need to make that change? (If yes, I will correct the I-D along those lines.)

comments.author: becarpenter
comments.body: The IAB would need to make that change _if they wanted to_.  (2850 is a BCP, so this would also require its own IETF consensus.)

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
Yes, if we want that change, the IAB would need to be involved and RFC2850 would need to be updated. RFC2850 is an IAB-stream BCP and I think we recent concluded that this shouldn't exist and BCPs need to go on the IETF stream. As such we could probably also change it by community consensus, however, I think the process for documents like this should be that they go through the IAB process first, get IAB approval, and then go into the community process.

However, I also don't think we should change that. IAB membership doesn't imply any specific tasks/work except voting; voting should always stay with the IETF Chair and if the IETF Chair is not available, the IETF Chair will simply not participate in the vote. For the exchange between the IAB and IESG we have the liaison.

Tones down the dramatic language in the chair stand-in draft and adds guidance for short absences.
